user.title: Heat Pump Optimizer Setup
user.description: Choose which Home Assistant entities the optimizer reads. Clear a field to stop using that sensor. Only the price token and weather forecast are required; every other sensor makes the model more accurate but is optional.

data_description.name: Shown in front of every sensor this integration creates.
data_description.tibber_token: Used to read your hourly electricity prices. Create one at developer.tibber.com. Leave as-is unless it has changed.
data_description.weather_entity: Where the outdoor temperature, wind and rain forecast comes from. The optimizer plans 24 hours ahead, so a forecast is required.
data_description.indoor_temp_entity: Optional. The actual room temperature. Without it the optimizer trusts its own model, which drifts over time.
data_description.outdoor_temp_entity: Optional. A local outdoor thermometer is more accurate than the forecast for the current hour.
data_description.heat_pump_switch_entity: Optional. A switch used to turn the heat pump off during expensive hours.
data_description.solar_radiation_entity: Optional. Sunshine in W/m2. Lets the optimizer skip heating before a sunny afternoon that will warm the house for free.
data_description.floor_return_temp_entity: Optional. Water temperature coming back from the floor loops, used to gauge how much heat the slab is holding.
data_description.lower_floor_temp_entity: Optional, two-zone only. A real thermometer in the lower zone. Without one the lower floor is inferred from the floor return water, which runs several degrees warmer than the room and makes the zone look warmer than it is.
data_description.dhw_temp_entity: Optional but recommended. The real tank temperature. Also lets a manual hot water boost reset the anti-legionella timer.
data_description.buffer_tank_temp_entity: Optional. When set, the integration learns how fast the buffer tank loses heat instead of relying on the configured estimate.
data_description.ecl110_displace_set_topic: MQTT topic the parallel heat-curve offset is published to. Leave blank if you do not have a Danfoss ECL110.
data_description.ecl110_command_topic: Only needed for older setups that expect a JSON payload instead.
data_description.ecl110_state_topic: MQTT topic the controller reports its current state on.
data_description.ecl110_mqtt_retain: Keeps the last offset on the broker so the controller picks it up after a restart.
data_description.ecl110_displace_min: How far the heat curve may be shifted down during expensive hours.
data_description.ecl110_displace_max: How far the heat curve may be shifted up when storing cheap heat.
data_description.ecl110_pid_time_constant_hours: Roughly how long the controller takes to act on a new offset. Used so the optimizer does not ask for changes faster than the system can follow.
data_description.solar_forecast_source: Where to get solar irradiance from. "Weather entity" uses your weather integration, which often does not publish irradiance at all. "Open-Meteo" fetches a free forecast for the location below; no account is needed.
data_description.solar_location: Coordinate used for the Open-Meteo irradiance forecast. Defaults to your Home Assistant home location. Only used when the source is Open-Meteo.

temperature.title: Temperature Settings
temperature.description: How warm you want the house, and how far the optimizer may drift from that to save money. The gap between the target and the minimum is what makes savings possible: the wider it is, the more the house can coast through expensive hours.

data_description.target_temperature: What you actually want the house to sit at. The optimizer aims for this and only drifts away from it to avoid expensive hours.
data_description.min_temperature: A hard floor. The house is never allowed below this, no matter how expensive electricity gets. A wider gap to the target means more room to save.
data_description.max_temperature: A hard ceiling. Caps how far ahead the optimizer may pre-heat the house during cheap hours.
data_description.comfort_temp_night: Preferred temperature overnight. Setting this a degree or two lower saves money and usually improves sleep.
data_description.day_start_hour: Hour of the morning when the daytime temperature takes over.
data_description.day_end_hour: Hour of the evening when the night-time temperature takes over.

thermal.title: Thermal Model & Optimization
thermal.description: Configure your house's thermal properties and heat pump. Default values work for a typical well-insulated Scandinavian house with slab floor heating. Adjust if needed.

data.price_weight: How hard to chase low prices
data.comfort_weight: How strictly to hold the temperature

data_description.house_thermal_mass: How much heat the building fabric stores per degree. Higher means the house holds its temperature longer and can coast further through expensive hours. Roughly 3 kWh/°C for a light timber house, 8 or more for heavy masonry.
data_description.house_heat_loss_coefficient: How fast the house loses heat per degree of difference to outside. Multiply by the indoor-outdoor gap to get the heating power needed: 0.25 kW/°C at 20 degrees difference means about 5 kW.
data_description.slab_thermal_mass: Heat stored in the concrete slab per degree. This is the buffer that lets floor heating be switched off during price peaks without the room getting cold.
data_description.slab_heat_transfer: How quickly heat moves from the slab into the room. Lower values mean a slow, sluggish floor that has to be charged further in advance.
data_description.heat_pump_cop_nominal: Units of heat produced per unit of electricity under normal conditions. Check the data sheet; 3 to 4 is typical for air-to-water, 4 to 5 for ground source.
data_description.heat_pump_max_power: Electrical input at full output. Caps how much cheap electricity can be stored per hour.
data_description.heat_pump_min_power: Lowest electrical input the pump can run at without cycling on and off.
data_description.optimization_interval: How often the plan is recalculated against fresh prices and weather. More often reacts quicker but does more work.
data_description.price_weight: Higher means the optimizer works harder to move heating into cheap hours, at the cost of letting the temperature swing more.
data_description.comfort_weight: The counterweight to the setting above, and the most effective knob you have. It is measured against the range you allow, so widening that range makes the optimizer bolder. Around 5 lets the house drift freely inside your allowed range for the biggest savings; 10 keeps it noticeably closer to target; 20 or more behaves almost like an ordinary thermostat.

zones.title: Two-Zone & Solar Configuration
zones.description: Optional: Configure two-zone heating (upper floor radiators + lower floor slab) and solar heat gain parameters. Leave defaults if you don't need the two-zone model.

data.radiator_power_fraction: Share of heat going to radiators
data.solar_heat_gain_coefficient: How much sunlight the windows let through

data_description.upper_floor_thermal_mass: Two-zone systems only. Heat stored per degree in the radiator-heated upper floor. Usually much lower than the slab, so this zone reacts faster.
data_description.lower_floor_thermal_mass: Two-zone systems only. Heat stored per degree in the slab-heated lower floor.
data_description.upper_floor_heat_loss: Two-zone systems only. How fast the upper floor loses heat per degree of difference to outside.
data_description.lower_floor_heat_loss: Two-zone systems only. How fast the lower floor loses heat per degree of difference to outside.
data_description.inter_zone_heat_transfer: How much heat drifts between the two floors. Higher values mean heating one floor warms the other as well, typical for an open stairwell.
data_description.radiator_power_fraction: Two-zone systems only. 0 means all heat goes to the floor slab, 1 means all of it goes to the radiators. 0.4 means 40 percent to radiators.
data_description.upper_floor_area_ratio: Share of the total floor area that sits upstairs. 0.5 means the two floors are the same size.
data_description.buffer_tank_volume: Litres. The tank between the heat pump and the heating circuits. Larger tanks store more cheap heat.
data_description.window_area: Square metres of glazing that gets direct sun. Used to predict free solar heating.
data_description.solar_orientation_factor: How well the windows face the sun over a day. 1.0 suits mostly south-facing glazing; lower it for east or west facing windows that only catch part of the day.
data_description.solar_heat_gain_coefficient: 0.6 is typical for modern triple glazing. Higher means more free heat on sunny days.

dhw.title: Domestic Hot Water (DHW) Configuration
dhw.description: Tell the optimizer when you actually need hot water. It then guarantees a usable tank temperature during those periods and heats the water in the cheapest hours beforehand. Outside those periods the tank may cool, so nothing is spent keeping water hot that nobody uses.

data.dhw_setpoint: Highest tank temperature to charge to
data.dhw_schedule_enabled: Only guarantee hot water at set times

data_description.dhw_schedule_enabled: On: hot water is guaranteed only during the times below, and the tank may cool down in between. Off: the tank is kept hot around the clock, which costs noticeably more.
data_description.dhw_windows: 24-hour times separated by commas, for example 06:00-08:30, 17:00-22:00. The tank is heated in the cheapest hours before each period. Leave empty to let the integration learn your habits from actual usage.
data_description.dhw_min_temperature: The temperature the tank is guaranteed to reach during the periods above. Around 45 C is enough for a normal shower.
data_description.dhw_idle_min_temperature: How cold the tank is allowed to get outside those periods. Lower saves more. The default is roughly room temperature, meaning no energy is spent at all.
data_description.dhw_setpoint: An upper limit on charging, not a target. The tank is only filled this high when storing extra cheap heat pays off. It is never heated to this just for the sake of it.
data_description.dhw_tank_volume: Litres. A larger tank stores more cheap electricity and can skip more expensive hours.
data_description.dhw_daily_consumption: Roughly how many litres of hot water your household uses per day. Used to work out how much to store before each period.
data_description.dhw_cooling_rate: How fast the tank cools when nobody uses hot water, measured at 45 C in a 20 C room. This is only a starting point: the integration measures your tank's actual cooling and refines it automatically. A tank that holds heat well can be charged further ahead of time, so more of the heating lands in cheap hours.
data_description.dhw_legionella_enabled: Because the tank is now allowed to stay cool for long stretches, it is periodically heated hot enough to kill legionella bacteria. Strongly recommended.
data_description.dhw_legionella_interval_days: How often the disinfection heat-up runs. It is placed in the cheapest hour before each deadline.

weather_sensitivity.title: Weather Sensitivity Parameters
weather_sensitivity.description: Configure how wind and rain affect heat loss predictions. Higher wind sensitivity = more pre-heating before windy periods.

data_description.wind_sensitivity_factor: How much extra heat the house loses per m/s of wind. Raise it if the house noticeably cools down on windy days, so the optimizer pre-heats beforehand.
data_description.rain_heat_loss_multiplier: Extra heat loss while it is raining. 1.0 means rain makes no difference.

error.invalid_tibber_token: That Tibber token was not accepted. Check it at developer.tibber.com and try again.
error.invalid_dhw_windows: Those time frames could not be read. Use 24-hour times separated by commas, for example "06:00-08:30, 17:00-22:00".
error.dhw_min_too_close: A hot water minimum this close to the setpoint leaves the tank no working band; keep it at least 5 \u00b0C below the setpoint.

abort.already_configured: This integration is already set up.

init.title: Heat Pump Optimizer options
init.description: Pick the group of settings you want to change. Sensors, building physics and control hardware live under Advanced settings.

advanced.title: Advanced settings
advanced.description: Settings you typically touch once: sensors, the building and its thermal model, solar panels, self-learning and the control hardware.

setup_overview.title: Your system, as configured
setup_overview.description:
What the optimizer believes your system is, from the current configuration. An empty slot is shown as empty on purpose — it is a sensor this setup could use and does not have.

{setup_summary}

data_description.solar_location: Coordinate used for the Open-Meteo irradiance forecast. Defaults to your Home Assistant home location. Only used when the source is Open-Meteo.
data_description.heat_pump_power_entity: Actual electrical draw. Without it the integration only knows what it asked the pump to do. With it, efficiency becomes measurable, predicted costs get a real counterpart to check against, and a wood furnace can be detected reliably. Watts or kilowatts both work.
data_description.heat_pump_energy_entity: A cumulative kWh meter, if you have one. More accurate than adding up power readings between updates, which misses short compressor runs.
data_description.house_power_entity: Total consumption at the meter. A capacity tariff is billed on the whole house, not on the heat pump alone, so without this the peak the optimizer avoids is only part of the real one.

comfort.title: Comfort and temperatures
comfort.description: How warm you want the house, and how far the optimizer may drift from that to save money. The gap between the target and the minimum is what makes savings possible: the wider it is, the more the house can coast through expensive hours.

data.mold_guard_enabled: Keep cold surfaces below mold humidity

data_description.target_temperature: What you actually want the house to sit at. The optimizer aims for this and only drifts away from it to avoid expensive hours.
data_description.min_temperature: A hard floor. The house is never allowed below this, no matter how expensive electricity gets. A wider gap to the target means more room to save.
data_description.max_temperature: A hard ceiling. Caps how far ahead the optimizer may pre-heat the house during cheap hours.
data_description.comfort_temp_night: Preferred temperature overnight. Setting this a degree or two lower saves money and usually improves sleep.
data_description.day_start_hour: Hour of the morning when the daytime temperature takes over.
data_description.day_end_hour: Hour of the evening when the night-time temperature takes over.
data_description.mold_guard_enabled: The coldest spot in the house — a window reveal, a corner behind a wardrobe — sits well below room temperature, and mold starts growing where its surface humidity stays above 80%. With this on, the optimizer will not coast the house below the temperature that keeps that spot safe, computed from the measured indoor humidity and the outdoor forecast. Needs the humidity sensor below; it never heats past your comfort target — persistent high humidity is a ventilation problem, not a heating one.
data_description.indoor_humidity_entity: A relative humidity sensor in the living space. Without one the mold guard stays off regardless of the switch.
data_description.thermal_bridge_frsi: How cold your worst surface gets, as a fraction: surface = outdoor + fRsi × (room − outdoor). 0.75 is the Swedish building-code guidance; lower means a colder worst spot and a more cautious guard.

hot_water.title: Hot water
hot_water.description: Tell the optimizer when you actually need hot water. It then guarantees a usable tank temperature during those periods and heats the water in the cheapest hours beforehand. Outside those periods the tank may cool, so nothing is spent keeping water hot that nobody uses.

data.dhw_schedule_enabled: Only guarantee hot water at set times
data.dhw_setpoint: Highest tank temperature to charge to
data.dhw_free_disinfection_enabled: Credit disinfection from any heat source
data.dhw_elastic_legionella_enabled: Let the anti-legionella cycle pick a cheap day
data.vvc_lead_minutes: Start circulation before a time frame

data_description.dhw_schedule_enabled: On: hot water is guaranteed only during the times below, and the tank may cool down in between. Off: the tank is kept hot around the clock, which costs noticeably more.
data_description.dhw_windows: 24-hour times separated by commas, for example 06:00-08:30, 17:00-22:00. The tank is heated in the cheapest hours before each period. Leave empty to let the integration learn your habits from actual usage.
data_description.dhw_min_temperature: The temperature the tank is guaranteed to reach during the periods above. Around 45 C is enough for a normal shower.
data_description.dhw_idle_min_temperature: How cold the tank is allowed to get outside those periods. Lower saves more. The default is roughly room temperature, meaning no energy is spent at all.
data_description.dhw_setpoint: An upper limit on charging, not a target. The tank is only filled this high when storing extra cheap heat pays off. It is never heated to this just for the sake of it.
data_description.dhw_tank_volume: Litres. A larger tank stores more cheap electricity and can skip more expensive hours.
data_description.dhw_daily_consumption: Roughly how many litres of hot water your household uses per day. Used to work out how much to store before each period.
data_description.dhw_cooling_rate: How fast the tank cools when nobody uses hot water, measured at 45 C in a 20 C room. This is only a starting point: the integration measures your tank's actual cooling and refines it automatically. A tank that holds heat well can be charged further ahead of time, so more of the heating lands in cheap hours.
data_description.dhw_legionella_enabled: Because the tank is now allowed to stay cool for long stretches, it is periodically heated hot enough to kill legionella bacteria. Strongly recommended.
data_description.dhw_legionella_interval_days: How often the disinfection heat-up runs. It is placed in the cheapest hour before each deadline.
data_description.dhw_inlet_temp: Yearly average temperature of the cold water refilling the tank. The Swedish default of 10 °C is right for most homes; change it only if you have measured yours.
data_description.dhw_inlet_seasonal_amplitude: How many degrees the incoming water swings around that average over the year — coldest in late February, warmest in late summer. Leave at 0 to treat it as constant.
data_description.dhw_inlet_entity: A temperature sensor on the incoming cold water pipe. When set, its live reading is used instead of the model above.
data_description.greywater_recovery_effectiveness: If a drain water heat recovery unit pre-warms the incoming water, the fraction of drain heat it returns. 0 means none installed.
data_description.dhw_quantile_targets_enabled: Learn how much hot water each time frame actually uses on a heavy day, and make the tank ready for that instead of for the average day. Needs a tank temperature sensor, configured hot water time frames, and a couple of weeks of evidence.
data_description.dhw_free_disinfection_enabled: If a wood boiler, solar coil or immersion heater already gets the tank to the anti-legionella temperature and holds it there, count that as a completed cycle instead of running another one.
data_description.dhw_elastic_legionella_enabled: Allow the anti-legionella cycle to run a day or two early when electricity is unusually cheap, instead of always waiting for its deadline. The deadline is still always honoured.
data_description.dhw_legionella_min_interval_days: Never run anti-legionella cycles closer together than this, even on very cheap days.
data_description.shower_flow_lpm: Your shower head's flow. Only used to translate the tank's content into shower minutes on the Mixed Hot Water sensor.
data_description.vvc_pump_entity: A switch controlling the hot water circulation (VVC) loop pump. When set, the pump only runs during your hot water time frames, plus the lead time below.
data_description.vvc_lead_minutes: How long before a hot water time frame the circulation pump starts, so the loop is already hot when the time frame opens.
data_description.space_circulation_pump_entity: A switch controlling the heating circulation pump. When set, the pump is paused only in slots that are provably idle and warm — it always runs when heat is planned, when it is freezing outside, or when any room is near its comfort floor.

building.title: Heating system and heat storage
building.description: Everything between the heat sources and the emitters: the mixing valve, the buffer tank as a store, and the wood furnace tank with its probes. Leave the valve at "No mixing valve" if you do not have one — the model is already correct for that case. The valve settings only take effect with the two-zone model configured.

data.valve_outlet_temp_entity: Temperature after the wood/heat-pump mixing valve (optional)
data.dhw_wood_coil_enabled: Hot water refilled through the wood tank

data_description.mixing_valve_mode: "Set by hand" is a valve you configure yourself; tell the integration below what you set it to. "Read from a sensor" means the integration can see the target but not change it. "Commanded by the optimizer" writes the recommended target to the valve's own controller through the control entity below.
data_description.mixing_valve_target: The indoor temperature the valve holds. Leave at 0 to use the top of your comfort band, which is the recommended setting: the building charges first at no efficiency cost, and the tank takes only the surplus.
data_description.mixing_valve_target_entity: Optional. Reads the valve's target rather than using the fixed value above.
data_description.mixing_valve_write_entity: Required for "Commanded by the optimizer": the number or climate entity your valve's controller exposes. The optimizer writes its recommended target there after each planning cycle, and only when the answer changes.
data_description.buffer_tank_volume: Litres. The tank between the heat pump and the heating circuits. Larger tanks store more cheap heat.
data_description.buffer_max_temperature: The tank is never charged above this, however cheap electricity is.
data_description.valve_outlet_temp_entity: Temperature of the blended flow leaving the valve that mixes wood and heat-pump water. With the tank sensors it tells the plan how much of the heating a fire is covering right now, so electric heat can stand down by that much instead of all-or-nothing.
data_description.wood_tank_top_entity: Together with the bottom sensor this says how much a fire has left. A hot top over a cold bottom means the charge is nearly spent.
data_description.wood_tank_bottom_entity: See the top sensor. Both are needed for the remaining-energy estimate; one alone is read conservatively.
data_description.wood_tank_volume: The wood-side buffer tank, used to bound how much free heat a fire can still deliver.
data_description.dhw_wood_coil_enabled: The hot water tank's cold-water inlet passes through a coil in the wood buffer tank, so refill water arrives preheated when that tank is hot. Only takes effect when the wood tank is modelled as its own store.

tuning.title: Savings vs comfort
tuning.description: The trade-off between a cheap bill and a rock-steady temperature. If the house feels too cool during price peaks, raise how strictly the temperature is held. If you want bigger savings and can live with more variation, lower it.

data.price_weight: How hard to chase low prices
data.comfort_weight: How strictly to hold the temperature
data.confidence_margins_enabled: Hold a safety margin where the model is unsure
data.wear_autotune_enabled: Let realised wear tune the cycling cost
data.price_tiles_enabled: Refresh price tiles after each solve

data_description.price_weight: Higher means the optimizer works harder to move heating into cheap hours, at the cost of letting the temperature swing more.
data_description.comfort_weight: The counterweight to the setting above, and the most effective knob you have. It is measured against the range you allow, so widening that range makes the optimizer bolder. Around 5 lets the house drift freely inside your allowed range for the biggest savings; 10 keeps it noticeably closer to target; 20 or more behaves almost like an ordinary thermostat.
data_description.optimization_interval: How often the plan is recalculated against fresh prices and weather. More often reacts quicker but does more work.
data_description.compressor_cycling_cost: Discourages plans that switch on and off repeatedly. Leave at 0 unless you have reason to think your unit is cycling too much; the planned start count is published on the plan sensors so you can look before deciding.
data_description.price_risk_lambda: Beyond the published horizon prices are estimated from your learned daily shape. This adds a premium to those guesses proportional to how wrong they have tended to be, so the plan stops treating a guessed cheap night as bankable. 0 trusts the guesses at face value, as before.
data_description.confidence_margins_enabled: A plan that promises 19.0 °C twelve hours ahead rests on a twelve-hour prediction, and the optimizer knows from its own history how wrong those get. With this on, the comfort floor rises by exactly that expected error — capped at 0.8 °C and shrinking to nothing as accuracy improves — so deep price-riding coasts are taken only where the model has earned the trust.
data_description.compressor_replacement_cost: What a compressor swap costs, including labour. Divided by the rated starts below it prices every realised compressor start; leave at 0 to keep the start counter pure observation with no money attached.
data_description.compressor_rated_starts: How many starts the manufacturer rates the compressor for. The replacement cost above is spread over this number.
data_description.wear_autotune_enabled: When on, the wear price per start (replacement cost divided by rated starts) becomes a floor under the compressor cycling cost above, so plans stop understating a cost you have made explicit. This is the only insight feature that changes plans.
data_description.price_tiles_enabled: After each scheduled optimization, price one what-if tile — target one degree lower, one degree higher, and power capped at 75 %, in rotation. Off by default because each tile is a full extra solve of real CPU.

heat_curve.title: Heat curve control (ECL110)
heat_curve.description: For Danfoss ECL110 controllers driven over MQTT. The optimizer shifts the heat curve up in cheap hours and down in expensive ones. Leave these blank if you do not have one.

data_description.ecl110_displace_set_topic: MQTT topic the parallel heat-curve offset is published to. Leave blank if you do not have a Danfoss ECL110.
data_description.ecl110_command_topic: Only needed for older setups that expect a JSON payload instead.

data_description.ecl110_displace_min: How far the heat curve may be shifted down during expensive hours.
data_description.ecl110_displace_max: How far the heat curve may be shifted up when storing cheap heat.
data_description.ecl110_pid_time_constant_hours: Roughly how long the controller takes to act on a new offset. Used so the optimizer does not ask for changes faster than the system can follow.

building_preset.title: Building type and emitters
building_preset.description: Answer three questions about the building and the thermal model's numbers are worked out for you. These are starting values only — the self-learning model refines them from how your house actually behaves, so they do not have to be exact. Leave this off if you have real values from an energy declaration and prefer to enter them directly on the thermal model page.

data.building_preset_enabled: Derive thermal values from the building type
data.building_structure: What the house is built from
data.solar_heat_gain_coefficient: How much sunlight the windows let through

data_description.building_preset_enabled: Turning this on overwrites the thermal mass and heat loss values on the House and heating system page.
data_description.building_structure: Heavy materials inside the insulation store heat, which is what lets the optimizer buy it cheaply and use it later.
data_description.building_era: Construction era is a good proxy for insulation standard, and a far better starting point than a single default.
data_description.heated_area_m2: Everything is scaled by this, so it is the number worth getting closest to right.
data_description.upper_floor_emitter: Radiators respond in minutes, floor heating in hours. That sets how far ahead heating can usefully be shifted.
data_description.lower_floor_emitter: A heated slab is a large store that gets actively charged, so it makes pre-heating both more valuable and more necessary.
data_description.window_area: Square metres of glazing that gets direct sun. Used to predict free solar heating.
data_description.solar_heat_gain_coefficient: 0.6 is typical for modern triple glazing. Higher means more free heat on sunny days.

thermal_model.title: Thermal model (expert)
thermal_model.description: The raw numbers behind the thermal model, otherwise only asked during setup. A field left empty keeps its current value and is never saved, so a single-zone house stays single-zone — and filling in the two-zone fields is how an existing install turns the two-zone model on.

data.radiator_power_fraction: Share of heat going to radiators

data_description.slab_heat_transfer: How quickly heat moves from the slab into the room. Lower values mean a slow, sluggish floor that has to be charged further in advance.
data_description.heat_pump_cop_nominal: Units of heat produced per unit of electricity under normal conditions. Check the data sheet; 3 to 4 is typical for air-to-water, 4 to 5 for ground source.
data_description.heat_pump_max_power: Electrical input at full output. Caps how much cheap electricity can be stored per hour.
data_description.heat_pump_min_power: Lowest electrical input the pump can run at without cycling on and off.
data_description.two_zone_mode: Off forces the single-zone model even though zone values are stored; On forces two-zone, using the values below or their defaults. Automatic keeps the old rule: two-zone as soon as any zone value has ever been saved — which can only ever turn it on, never off.
data_description.upper_floor_thermal_mass: Two-zone systems only. Heat stored per degree in the radiator-heated upper floor. Usually much lower than the slab, so this zone reacts faster.
data_description.lower_floor_thermal_mass: Two-zone systems only. Heat stored per degree in the slab-heated lower floor.
data_description.upper_floor_heat_loss: Two-zone systems only. How fast the upper floor loses heat per degree of difference to outside.
data_description.lower_floor_heat_loss: Two-zone systems only. How fast the lower floor loses heat per degree of difference to outside.
data_description.inter_zone_heat_transfer: How much heat drifts between the two floors. Higher values mean heating one floor warms the other as well, typical for an open stairwell.
data_description.radiator_power_fraction: Two-zone systems only. 0 means all heat goes to the floor slab, 1 means all of it goes to the radiators. 0.4 means 40 percent to radiators.
data_description.upper_floor_area_ratio: Share of the total floor area that sits upstairs. 0.5 means the two floors are the same size.
data_description.solar_orientation_factor: How well the windows face the sun over a day. 1.0 suits mostly south-facing glazing; lower it for east or west facing windows that only catch part of the day.

grid.title: Grid costs
grid.description: Costs that are not simply the price per kWh. Many Swedish grid companies also bill a monthly capacity charge based on your highest hours — which means stacking hot water and heating into the same cheap hour can cost more than it saves.

data.peak_tariff_enabled: My grid bill has a capacity charge
data.peak_tariff_price_per_kw: Capacity charge per kW per month
data.fuse_guard_enabled: Keep the plan under the main fuse

data_description.peak_tariff_price_per_kw: Take this from your grid invoice — it varies a lot between grid companies.
data_description.peak_tariff_peaks_averaged: Most Swedish tariffs average the three highest hours of the month. Check your invoice.
data_description.peak_tariff_window_minutes: Hourly for most tariffs. Some newer ones measure every 15 minutes, which is much less forgiving.
data_description.peak_tariff_months: For example "Nov-Mar". Empty means the tariff bills every month. Outside these months a peak contributes nothing to the bill, and the plan knows it.
data_description.peak_tariff_hours: For example "07:00-19:00". Empty means every hour counts in full. Outside these hours a peak counts at the off-peak factor below.
data_description.peak_tariff_weekdays_only: Many Swedish tariffs only bill weekday peaks. With this on, Saturday and Sunday count at the off-peak factor.
data_description.peak_tariff_offpeak_factor: 1.0 treats every hour the same, which is how it worked before. 0.5 is the common half-rate night peak; 0 makes off-peak hours free — night-time stacking then costs nothing in capacity, which is exactly the cheap-hour concentration this integration exists to find.
data_description.grid_fee_mode: The fee your grid company adds per kWh transferred. Tibber's price does not include it, so with it configured the plan finally sees the whole marginal price. "Rules" uses the schedule below; "Live sensor" follows an entity.
data_description.grid_fee_fixed: A flat fee added in every hour, on top of any rules. Take it from your grid invoice.
data_description.grid_fee_rules: One rule per line, for example "Nov-Mar Mon-Fri 06:00-22:00 = 0.25". Month, weekday and time parts are each optional; overlapping rules add together, which matches a base fee plus a high-load surcharge.
data_description.grid_fee_entity: A sensor reporting the current fee in SEK/kWh, for grids with dynamic fees. Its value is added to every planned hour.
data_description.contract_fixed_price: If you could have a fixed-price contract, its SEK/kWh. The Contract Comparison sensor then shows what this month would have cost on it. 0 leaves that column out.
data_description.main_fuse_amperes: The house's main fuse in amperes, from your grid contract. 0 leaves it unconfigured, which keeps the fuse advisor, the fuse guard and the headroom sensor dormant — there is no safe default to guess, and a wrong one would cap a bigger house.
data_description.fuse_guard_enabled: Caps the heat pump's planned power at what the fuse leaves after the rest of the house. If a cap would make the comfort floor unreachable, the plan says so on its sensors instead of silently going cold.
data_description.peak_guard_enabled: Watches the power meter live and, when the current metering window is projected to set a new billed peak, holds back electric hot water and nudges the heat curve down for the rest of that window. Needs a power meter; a cold tank or a breached comfort floor always wins over the guard.
data_description.peak_guard_margin_kw: How far below the billed threshold the guard starts acting. Larger catches more peaks and intervenes more often.

solar_pv.title: Solar panels
solar_pv.description: If you have solar, heating hot water or the buffer from surplus production beats exporting it at the compensation rate. Tell the optimizer about the array and it prices each hour at what consuming actually costs you.

data_description.pv_system_efficiency: Everything between sunlight and the meter: inverter losses, panel temperature, dirt, orientation. 0.8 is typical.
data_description.pv_export_price: What you are paid for an exported kWh. While you have surplus, that is what an extra kWh of heating really costs.
data_description.pv_export_price_entity: Use this instead if your compensation follows the spot price.

away.title: Away and holiday mode
away.description: A week away is the biggest single saving a heating system can offer. If you also say when you are coming back, the heat needed to warm the house again is bought in the cheapest hours beforehand instead of at whatever the price happens to be when you walk in.

data_description.away_presence_entity: A holiday toggle, a person or device tracker, or a calendar. The polarity is handled for you: a person being 'not home' and a holiday toggle being 'on' both mean away.
data_description.away_return_entity: Without this the house stays at the setback until you manually switch back, and warming up then costs whatever the current price is.
data_description.away_dhw_min_temperature: The anti-legionella cycle still runs, and is timed to finish before you get back.

learning.title: Self-learning and diagnostics
learning.description: Watchdogs and optional learning features. The sensor watchdog is on by default and protects everything else; the rest are off until you turn them on.

data.external_heat_detection_enabled: Detect a wood furnace or other heat source
data.external_heat_min_rise: Temperature rise that counts as evidence
data.external_heat_decay_minutes: How long to keep assuming it after it stops
data.comfort_learning_enabled: Learn my comfort preference from overrides
data.price_prior_enabled: Estimate prices past the published horizon
data.outage_recovery_enabled: Staggered recovery after a power cut
data.open_window_relax_enabled: Ease heating while a window is open
data.precip_type_enabled: Tell snow from rain in the forecast
data.snow_roof_factor_enabled: Assume less sun after heavy snowfall
data.capacity_curve_enabled: Plan within measured heat pump capacity
data.solar_aperture_learning_enabled: Learn how much sun the windows really admit
data.internal_gains_learning_enabled: Learn the household's daily heat rhythm
data.curve_learning_enabled: Learn a correction to the heat curve

data_description.staleness_watchdog_enabled: A dead battery leaves a perfectly normal-looking value in place forever. Left alone, the model learns from that flatline and the damage survives a restart. With this on, an old value is treated as missing and learning pauses instead.
data_description.staleness_max_age_scale: Raise this if you have sensors that deliberately report rarely and are being flagged unnecessarily.
data_description.external_heat_detection_enabled: Spots the tanks warming up when the heat pump is not running. While that is happening, planned electric hot water is held back — paying to heat water that is already being heated for free is the most expensive mistake available.
data_description.external_heat_entity: If you have a flue thermostat or a stove switch, use it. It is trusted over the automatic detection.
data_description.external_heat_min_rise: Raise this if normal operation triggers it. Missing a fire costs one unnecessary heating cycle; wrongly assuming one can leave you without hot water.
data_description.comfort_learning_enabled: Every time you override the temperature, you are saying the plan went too far in one direction. This slowly adjusts the comfort setting from that. The learned value is shown on its own sensor and there is a button to reset it.
data_description.system_identification_enabled: Lets the optimizer run a small deliberate heating step on a mild, cheap night to measure your house directly, instead of waiting weeks to infer it. The change is kept too small to notice and it stops if the temperature drifts.
data_description.price_prior_enabled: Tomorrow's prices arrive around 13:00. Before then the rest of the horizon used to be a flat repeat of the last price, which hides every cheap hour ahead. This learns your typical daily price shape and uses it instead, and the plan marks which hours are estimated.
data_description.outage_recovery_enabled: After an outage everything restarts at once — cold house, cold tank, the whole neighbourhood — which is exactly when a new monthly capacity peak gets set. With this on, a long gap in updates opens a two-hour recovery window where the capacity charge is taken seriously from the first kW and hot water queues 45 minutes behind space heating, unless the tank is genuinely low.
data_description.open_window_relax_enabled: The open-window detector always pauses learning — that part is free and always on. This additionally lowers the heating target by 1 °C while a window appears to be open, so the heat pump stops paying to heat the garden. Off by default because it moves real heat: a wrongly flagged window means a slightly cooler house.
data_description.immersion_feedback_enabled: When the tank's electric immersion element keeps stepping in, the plan is not heating water early enough. With this on, repeated immersion use raises the hot-water planning margin so the heat pump gets there first, and the extra cost shows up as its own line in the savings ledger.
data_description.precip_type_enabled: Rain soaks the building envelope and increases heat loss; snow does not. Without this, a snowy forecast is treated as rain and the plan buys heat for a wet wall that stays dry. Needs the Open-Meteo connection for the snow data.
data_description.snow_roof_factor_enabled: For two days after heavy snowfall, the modelled solar gain is halved — snow on roof glazing and low winter panes blocks the sun the plan was counting on. Deliberately crude: a factor and a holding period, not a melt model.
data_description.capacity_curve_enabled: The nameplate maximum is a laboratory number. This learns how much heat the pump has actually delivered at each outdoor temperature and plans within it, so a cold-snap plan stops promising output the machine has never produced. It can only trim optimism — at least 60% of nameplate always stays available.
data_description.solar_aperture_learning_enabled: Window area and shading are configured guesses. This compares sunny-hour predictions with what actually happened and scales the solar gain accordingly, between a third and double the configured value.
data_description.internal_gains_learning_enabled: People, cooking and appliances heat the house on a daily rhythm the flat constant cannot see. This learns a per-hour profile from dark-hour prediction errors, gently tethered to the configured value so it stays a refinement, not a rewrite.
data_description.curve_learning_enabled: Most heat curves were set once, conservatively, by an installer who never came back. This learns a standing correction from days that held comfort with room to spare — creeping cooler by at most half a degree per week, and snapping back to the installer's curve instantly on any comfort miss. It can only cool an over-hot curve, never heat.

error.invalid_tibber_token: That Tibber token was not accepted. Check it at developer.tibber.com and try again.
error.invalid_dhw_windows: Those time frames could not be read. Use 24-hour times separated by commas, for example "06:00-08:30, 17:00-22:00".
error.dhw_min_too_close: A hot water minimum this close to the setpoint leaves the tank no working band; keep it at least 5 \u00b0C below the setpoint.
error.invalid_grid_fee_rules: Those fee rules could not be read. One rule per line, like "Nov-Mar Mon-Fri 06:00-22:00 = 0.25".
error.invalid_peak_months: Those months could not be read. Use ranges like "Nov-Mar" or single months like "Jul".
error.invalid_peak_hours: Those hours could not be read. Use 24-hour ranges like "07:00-19:00".

options.timber_crawlspace: Timber frame, crawl space or suspended floor
options.timber_slab: Timber frame on a concrete slab
options.concrete_slab: Concrete or brick on a slab

cop_degradation.title: Heat pump efficiency has dropped
cop_degradation.description: The heat pump has been delivering about {shortfall_percent} % less heat per kWh than it used to under the same conditions, which is costing roughly {sek_month} SEK per month at recent prices. The usual suspects are a clogged filter, low refrigerant, or a defrost problem — worth a look before the season gets colder. This notice clears itself if efficiency recovers.

accuracy_drift.title: Learned model is drifting
accuracy_drift.description: The optimizer's predictions have been consistently off for several days, which usually means something about the house or the system changed faster than the learners can follow. Check that sensors read sensibly. If the plan has become noticeably worse, the "Restore learned snapshot" service rolls the learned model back to the last known-good weekly snapshot.

accuracy_drift_rolled_back.title: Learned model was restored from a snapshot
accuracy_drift_rolled_back.description: The optimizer's predictions drifted out of band for several days while all inputs looked healthy, so the learned model was automatically rolled back to the most recent known-good weekly snapshot. Nothing is required from you; this notice is here so the change is visible. If the drift was real — new radiators, changed insulation — the learners will simply relearn from the restored point.
